name: Present Bias
description: People place disproportionately high weight on immediate rewards/costs relative to future ones, leading to procrastination and undersaving.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to subscription cancellation flows, savings/goal-setting features, and any design encouraging deferred gratification.
prevalence_note: Well known in behavioral-design and fintech/wellness product circles specifically, less universally invoked than loss aversion or anchoring.

findings.description: Human time preferences are better described by a hyperbolic (quasi-hyperbolic, present-biased) discount function than by the classical exponential-discounting model of economics — implying people place disproportionately high weight on immediate rewards relative to future ones, explaining undersaving and self-control problems and motivating commitment-device interventions.

Present-biased preferences, combined with people's naivete or partial sophistication about their own future self-control problems, produce systematic procrastination on tasks with immediate costs/delayed benefits, and premature action on tasks with immediate benefits/delayed costs.

applications.title: Commitment and reminder nudges reduced stated intent to delay security updates
applications.description: Researchers ran two online experiments (1,000+ participants total) testing whether commitment devices could counter present bias in computer-security behavior. Adding a reminder option reduced stated intent to ignore an automatic-updates prompt by 57% in Study 1; in Study 2, a reminder option reduced willingness to ignore security updates by more than 40% for both Windows and Mac users, and a future-commitment option reduced ignore rates by about 25% for both. The same nudges increased willingness to enroll in two-factor authentication but did not improve uptake of automatic backup tools.
applications.ethical_note: Nudging users toward actions that directly protect their own security (installing patches) with no competing business interest is a clear case of user-beneficial design -- there is no persuasion-for-profit dimension here, only a genuine attempt to close the gap between people's security intentions and their present-biased follow-through.
